reason: DNA nucleotides and the nucleus are the clearest pairing for copying the genome.
expectation: The nucleotides will be used to copy the cell's DNA.

effect: The genome is copied, leaving cell growth and spindle construction to address.
reaction: The distinction between copying all chromosomes and making proteins is useful.
reason: Tubulin and spindle motors should work with the duplicated centrosomes to build the spindle.
expectation: A chromosome-separating spindle will form between the organizing centres.

effect: The spindle is built, and making two complete daughter cells is now a goal; cell growth remains unfinished.
reaction: The spindle picture makes clear that chromosomes have not yet separated.
reason: Phospholipids can expand the stem cell's membrane, contributing to its growth.
expectation: The cell will gain membrane material, possibly alongside its other growth requirements.

effect: The attempt instead combined phospholipids with proteins to make membrane vesicles, suggesting an intermediate for cell growth.
reaction: The vesicle intermediate was unexpected but fits the membrane-growth goal.
reason: The new vesicles may supply membrane to the growing stem cell.
expectation: The vesicles will contribute membrane to the cell as it grows.

effect: The vesicles enlarged the cell body, completing the growth goal; the copied genome and spindle still need to be brought together for division.
reaction: The growth picture usefully shows increased cytoplasm and organelles as well as membrane.
reason: The spindle must engage the copied chromosomes to separate them between daughter cells.
expectation: The spindle will engage the copied chromosomes, advancing their separation.

effect: The spindle separated the copied chromosomes into matching sets, but the cell still has one shared cytoplasm.
reaction: The distinction between chromosome separation and cell division is useful.
reason: The separated chromosome sets need to be brought together with the enlarged cell body before division.

choice.combine: Separated chromosome sets inside the cell

expectation: The enlarged cell will contain the separated chromosome sets, advancing division into two daughter cells.

alternatives.reason: Actin and myosin could help divide the cell body, but the separated chromosomes may need to be incorporated first.

effect: The enlarged cell now has two daughter nuclei, but its cytoplasm remains shared.
reaction: The separate nuclear and cytoplasmic stages are clear in the picture.
reason: Cortical actin and myosin can constrict the cell to divide its shared cytoplasm.

choice.with: Stem cell with two daughter nuclei

expectation: The cell will divide into two daughter stem cells, each with a nucleus.

effect: Actin and myosin divided the shared cytoplasm, completing the daughter-cell goal; both cells remain pluripotent under the model's self-renewal conditions.
reaction: The final picture plan clearly distinguishes two separate cells from the earlier shared cytoplasm.

mostWorthwhile.text: Separating the copied chromosomes was most worthwhile: the picture plan and explanation distinguish sister-chromatid separation from division of the cell itself.

leastWorthwhile.text: The spindle picture plan shows fibres, but the brief result does not explain how they attach to chromosomes; that connection would help a student unfamiliar with mitosis.

surprise.text: Phospholipids first combined with proteins to make membrane vesicles rather than being added directly to the cell. The vesicles then contributed to growth.

arbitrary.text: The vesicle intermediate was not obvious from the initial growth goal, although the compatibility feedback revealed it and its later use made sense.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: building division in stages made the distinction between genome copying, chromosome separation and cytoplasmic division interesting.
